title: Module Header and Imports
content: Documents the file's scope: extending the parent Erdos1155Problem.lean formalization to analyze the gap between the Bohman-Frieze-Lubetzky (BFL) $n^{3/2+o(1)}$ result and Erdős's conjectured $\Theta(n^{3/2})$. Imports all of Mathlib to access filters, real powers, simple graph clique theory, and topological convergence.
mathContext: Uses Mathlib's filter-based asymptotics: $\forall^\infty n$ means `Filter.Eventually` in `atTop`, and convergence uses `Filter.Tendsto` into `nhds`.

title: Triangle Predicates and Complete Graph Triangles
content:
Defines pointwise triangle predicates (`IsTriangle'`, `IsTriangleFree`) and proves their equivalence with Mathlib's `CliqueFree 3`. The forward direction extracts three vertices from a 3-clique via `card_eq_three`. The backward direction constructs a 3-element finset and verifies the clique condition by case analysis on all $3 \times 3 = 9$ vertex assignments.

`complete_has_triangles'` proves $K_n$ contains triangles for $n \geq 3$ by constructing the explicit triangle $(0, 1, 2)$ in `Fin n`. In the complete graph, all pairs are adjacent, so verifying the triangle condition reduces to verifying distinctness. This connects to Ramsey theory (see `ramseys-theorem`): Ramsey's theorem guarantees triangles in any sufficiently large 2-colored complete graph, while here we simply need the uncolored $K_n$ to contain a triangle (trivially true for $n \geq 3$).
mathContext:
A triangle in a simple graph $G$ is three distinct mutually adjacent vertices $a, b, c$ with edges $ab, bc, ac$. The equivalence $	ext{IsTriangleFree}(G) \iff G.	ext{CliqueFree}\,3$ bridges the pointwise and Mathlib definitions. The pointwise definition uses six conjuncts: $a 
eq b \wedge b 
eq c \wedge a 
eq c \wedge G.	ext{Adj}\,a\,b \wedge G.	ext{Adj}\,b\,c \wedge G.	ext{Adj}\,a\,c$.

title: Axiomatized f(n), BFL Bounds, and the Erdős Conjecture
content:
Axiomatizes the triangle removal function $f(n)$ with basic properties ($0 \leq f(n) \leq \binom{n}{2}$) and the BFL (2015) bounds: for any $\varepsilon > 0$, eventually $n^{3/2-\varepsilon} \leq f(n) \leq n^{3/2+\varepsilon}$.

The **Erdős conjecture** (`erdos_1155_conjecture`) is formalized as: $\exists c_1 \leq c_2$ with $0 < c_1$ such that $c_1 n^{3/2} \leq f(n) \leq c_2 n^{3/2}$ eventually. The gap: BFL gives sub-polynomial bounds $n^{\pm\varepsilon}$ on the ratio $f(n)/n^{3/2}$, while the conjecture needs constant bounds.

**Axiomatization strategy**: The 5 axioms encode externally established results (Mantel's theorem, BFL bounds, the definition of $f$) while all structural theorems are fully proved from these axioms. This cleanly separates hard probabilistic analysis from combinatorial-logical structure.
mathContext: $\text{erdos\_1155\_conjecture} := \exists c_1, c_2,\; 0 < c_1 \leq c_2 \wedge \forall^\infty n,\; c_1 n^{3/2} \leq f(n) \leq c_2 n^{3/2}$. The requirement $c_1 \leq c_2$ is built into the definition.

title: BFL Sandwich and Conjecture Implications
content:
`bfl_sandwich` combines the two BFL bounds into a single statement: for any $\varepsilon > 0$, eventually $n^{3/2-\varepsilon} \leq f(n) \leq n^{3/2+\varepsilon}$, using `Filter.Eventually.and`.

The implication theorems prove Conjecture $\Longrightarrow$ BFL in both directions: `conjecture_implies_bfl_upper` shows $f(n) \leq C n^{3/2} \leq n^{\varepsilon} n^{3/2}$ for large $n$, and the lower direction is symmetric. The key idea: a fixed constant $C$ is eventually dominated by $n^{\varepsilon}$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$, since $n^{\varepsilon} \to \infty$.

The proof technique for `conjecture_implies_bfl_upper` is instructive: given $C > 0$, one needs $C \leq n^\varepsilon$ for large $n$. The bound $n \geq \lceil C^{1/\varepsilon} \rceil + 1$ suffices, using $n^\varepsilon \geq (C^{1/\varepsilon})^\varepsilon = C$. This constant-to-sub-polynomial reduction is the core of the BFL-conjecture gap.
mathContext: The gap: BFL gives $n^{-\varepsilon} \leq f(n)/n^{3/2} \leq n^{\varepsilon}$ (bounds that grow/shrink with $n$), while the conjecture needs $c_1 \leq f(n)/n^{3/2} \leq c_2$ (fixed constants independent of $n$). The proof uses $\text{rpow\_add}$: $n^{3/2+\varepsilon} = n^\varepsilon \cdot n^{3/2}$, so $f(n) \leq C n^{3/2} \leq n^\varepsilon n^{3/2} = n^{3/2+\varepsilon}$.

title: One-Sided Theta Bounds: Upper and Lower
content:
`upper_theta_bound` and `lower_theta_bound` formalize the two independent components of $\Theta(n^{3/2})$. The upper bound asks for $C > 0$ with $f(n) \leq C n^{3/2}$ eventually; the lower bound asks for $c > 0$ with $c n^{3/2} \leq f(n)$ eventually.

Separating these is strategically motivated: the BFL proof establishes both bounds simultaneously via a single differential equation analysis, but a future proof of the full conjecture might establish them independently. The upper bound is often considered harder: it requires showing that the triangle removal process terminates with at most $O(n^{3/2})$ edges, ruling out slow-terminating configurations.
mathContext:
$\text{upper\_theta\_bound} := \exists C > 0,\; f(n) \leq C n^{3/2}$ eventually.
$\text{lower\_theta\_bound} := \exists c > 0,\; c n^{3/2} \leq f(n)$ eventually.

The conjecture is their conjunction with the consistency requirement $c \leq C$.

title: Conjecture Decomposition into Independent Bounds
content:
`conjecture_iff_both_bounds`: $f(n) = \Theta(n^{3/2})$ iff both $f(n) = O(n^{3/2})$ AND $f(n) = \Omega(n^{3/2})$ hold independently. The non-trivial direction combines the bounds and proves $c_1 \leq c_2$ by contradiction: if $c_1 > c_2$, then $c_1 n^{3/2} \leq f(n) \leq c_2 n^{3/2}$ forces $c_1 \leq c_2$ for large $n$.

This decomposition is strategically important: it means the $O$ and $\Omega$ bounds can be attacked independently, and proving either constitutes concrete progress toward the full conjecture. Analogous decompositions appear throughout asymptotic analysis — the Szemerédi regularity lemma (see `szemeredi-regularity`) decomposes graph structure into pseudorandom and structured components in a similar spirit.
mathContext: $f(n) = \Theta(n^{3/2}) \iff f(n) = O(n^{3/2}) \wedge f(n) = \Omega(n^{3/2})$. The non-trivial direction: given $c n^{3/2} \leq f(n) \leq C n^{3/2}$, assume $c > C$. Then for large $n$, $c n^{3/2} \leq f(n) \leq C n^{3/2} < c n^{3/2}$, contradiction. So $c \leq C$.

title: Exponent Characterization: 3/2 is Critical
content:
`bfl_exponent_is_three_halves`: for any $\alpha > 3/2$, $f(n) \leq n^\alpha$ eventually (substituting $\varepsilon = \alpha - 3/2$). `bfl_lower_tight`: NO exponent $\beta < 3/2$ gives $f(n) \leq n^\beta$ eventually (contradiction via BFL lower bound).

Together: $3/2$ is the exact critical exponent separating polynomial upper bounds from growth rates. This is the exponent-level content of BFL, abstracting away the sub-polynomial corrections.
mathContext: $f(n) = O(n^\alpha)$ for all $\alpha > 3/2$, but $f(n) \neq O(n^\beta)$ for any $\beta < 3/2$. The critical exponent $3/2$ is exact: it is the infimum of exponents $\alpha$ for which $f(n) = O(n^\alpha)$.

title: Small Values, Base Cases, and BFL Ratio Reformulation
content:
Establishes trivial bounds for small $n$: $f(0) \leq 0$, $f(1) \leq 0$, $f(2) \leq 1$ from $f(n) \leq n(n-1)/2$.

`bfl_ratio_characterization` reformulates BFL as: the ratio $f(n)/n^{3/2}$ is eventually in $[n^{-\varepsilon}, n^{\varepsilon}]$, making the gap with the conjecture (constant bounds on the ratio) maximally transparent. This ratio formulation is the sharpest way to see the BFL-conjecture gap: BFL allows the ratio to drift to 0 or $\infty$ at sub-polynomial speed, while the conjecture pins it between constants.
mathContext: Ratio reformulation: BFL $\iff R(n) = f(n)/n^{3/2} \in [n^{-\varepsilon}, n^{\varepsilon}]$ eventually. The conjecture needs $R(n) \in [c_1, c_2]$ with constants.

title: Limit Convergence Implies the Conjecture
content:
`limit_implies_conjecture`: if $f(n)/n^{3/2} \to L > 0$, the conjecture holds with $c_1 = L/2$, $c_2 = 3L/2$. The proof uses the closed interval $[L/2, 3L/2]$ as a neighborhood of $L$ in $\mathbb{R}$ via `Icc_mem_nhds`, then applies `Filter.Tendsto.eventually` to get the ratio into this interval for all large $n$.

This is the strongest sufficient condition: convergence of the ratio implies the conjecture with explicit constants derived from the limit. Simulations suggest $L \approx 1.2$, but this is not rigorously established — proving (or disproving) convergence is arguably the deepest open question about the triangle removal process.
mathContext: If $\lim_{n \to \infty} f(n)/n^{3/2} = L > 0$, then for large $n$: $L/2 \leq f(n)/n^{3/2} \leq 3L/2$, so $c_1 = L/2$ and $c_2 = 3L/2$ satisfy the conjecture. The Lean proof: `Icc_mem_nhds (by linarith) (by linarith)` shows $[L/2, 3L/2] \in \text{nhds}(L)$.

title: Weaker Sufficient Condition: Bounded Limsup/Liminf
content:
`limsup_liminf_condition` formalizes a weaker sufficient condition: there exist $c, C > 0$ such that $c \leq f(n)/n^{3/2} \leq C$ eventually. This doesn't require convergence of the ratio — the ratio can oscillate, as long as it stays in a compact interval $(0, \infty)$.

`limsup_liminf_implies_conjecture` proves this implies the full conjecture. The proof combines the two one-sided bounds and shows $c \leq C$ by contradiction (same technique as in `conjecture_iff_both_bounds`). This shows the conjecture is equivalent to a compactness condition on the ratio sequence — the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem then guarantees convergent subsequences, though not convergence of the sequence itself.
mathContext: $\text{limsup\_liminf\_condition} := (\exists C > 0,\; R(n) \leq C \text{ eventually}) \wedge (\exists c > 0,\; c \leq R(n) \text{ eventually})$ where $R(n) = f(n)/n^{3/2}$. This is equivalent to the conjecture: $R(n) \in [c, C]$ eventually.

title: Lower Exponent: f Exceeds Any Sub-3/2 Power
content:
`bfl_eventually_exceeds_power`: for any $\alpha < 3/2$, eventually $n^\alpha \leq f(n)$. Proved by taking $\varepsilon = 3/2 - \alpha$ in the BFL lower bound. Special cases: $f$ is superlinear ($\alpha = 1$) and grows faster than $n^{5/4}$.

This is the 'lower critical exponent' result: $f(n) = \omega(n^\alpha)$ for every $\alpha < 3/2$, meaning no sub-$3/2$ power bound is eventually valid from above.
mathContext: For $\alpha < 3/2$: take $\varepsilon = 3/2 - \alpha > 0$, then $n^{3/2 - \varepsilon} = n^\alpha \leq f(n)$ eventually. This shows $f(n) = \omega(n^\alpha)$ for all $\alpha < 3/2$.

title: Mantel/Turán Connection
content:
Connects the triangle removal process to Mantel's theorem (1907): the terminal graph is triangle-free, so $f(n) \leq n^2/4$. The BFL bound $f(n) \leq n^{7/4}$ (taking $\varepsilon = 1/4$) is much tighter. The hierarchy: $n^{3/2} \ll n^{7/4} \ll n^2/4$.

Mantel's theorem is the $r = 2$ case of Turán's theorem (1941): the maximum number of edges in a $K_{r+1}$-free graph on $n$ vertices is $(1 - 1/r)n^2/2$, achieved by the complete $r$-partite Turán graph $T(n, r)$. The triangle supersaturation phenomenon (Razborov 2010, flag algebras) quantifies how many triangles a dense graph must contain — this governs the early stages of the removal process when triangle density is high. The Szemerédi regularity lemma (see `szemeredi-regularity`) provides the deterministic counterpart: the triangle removal lemma says graphs with $o(n^3)$ triangles can be made triangle-free by removing $o(n^2)$ edges.
mathContext: Mantel's theorem (1907): a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices has at most $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ edges, achieved by $K_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor, \lceil n/2 \rceil}$. Applied: $f(n) \leq n^2/4$. BFL's $n^{7/4}$ bound (taking $\varepsilon = 1/4$ in the upper bound) improves this by a factor of $n^{1/4}$. The conjectured $n^{3/2}$ improves further by $n^{1/4}$.

title: Strict Hierarchy: Conjecture > BFL > Grable
content:
Proves the strict weakening chain: Conjecture $\Longrightarrow$ BFL $\Longrightarrow$ Grable. Each step loses information about the multiplicative constant: the conjecture fixes constants, BFL allows sub-polynomial growth, and Grable allows polynomial growth ($n^{7/4+\varepsilon}$).

This hierarchy provides a roadmap for incremental progress: each strengthening requires tighter control of the multiplicative constants. Proving the conjecture means tightening BFL's sub-polynomial bounds to constants — the gap between $n^{\pm\varepsilon}$ and $O(1)$.

`hierarchy_bfl_implies_grable` extracts Grable's bound from BFL by setting $\varepsilon = 1/4 + \varepsilon'$: the BFL upper bound $f(n) \leq n^{3/2 + 1/4 + \varepsilon'} = n^{7/4 + \varepsilon'}$ recovers the Grable-type bound. The Lean proof: `rwa [show (3:ℝ)/2 + (1/4 + ε) = 7/4 + ε from by ring]`.
mathContext: Strict hierarchy: $\Theta(n^{3/2}) \Longrightarrow n^{3/2 \pm o(1)} \Longrightarrow n^{7/4+o(1)}$. Each weakening relaxes the multiplicative constant control. Quantitatively: the conjecture pins $R(n) = f(n)/n^{3/2} \in [c_1, c_2]$; BFL gives $R(n) \in [n^{-\varepsilon}, n^{\varepsilon}]$; Grable gives only $f(n) \leq n^{7/4+\varepsilon}$, i.e., $R(n) \leq n^{1/4+\varepsilon}$.

title: Ratio Tightness and Compactness Characterization
content:
`conjecture_tightness`: under the conjecture, $f(n)/(c_1 n^{3/2}) \in [1, c_2/c_1]$ eventually. `conjecture_ratio_bounded`: $f(n)/n^{3/2} \in [c_1, c_2]$ eventually.

Together these characterize the conjecture as: the normalized ratio $f(n)/n^{3/2}$ has a compact limit set in $(0, \infty)$ — a topological reformulation of the number-theoretic conjecture. This is the sharpest formulation of the BFL-conjecture gap: BFL says the ratio eventually avoids $\{0, \infty\}$ at sub-polynomial rate; the conjecture says it eventually stays in a compact interval.
mathContext: The conjecture is equivalent to $\{f(n)/n^{3/2}\}_{n \geq N}$ being bounded in $(0, \infty)$: a compactness condition. This is the sharpest formulation of the BFL-conjecture gap.
